s: Reading the spectrum: the peaks are at m/z = 12, 16, 28 and 44, with the base (tallest) peak at 44.
m/z 44 is the molecular ion CO₂⁺; 28 is CO⁺, 16 is O⁺ and 12 is C⁺ — fragments of carbon dioxide.
N₂ would give its molecular ion at 28; C₃H₈ (M = 44) would also give many hydrocarbon fragments at 15, 29, 43; CH₄ + N₂ would give peaks at 16 and 28 only. So the compound is CO₂.

¹⁶O has 8 protons and 8 neutrons, so its spin is zero and it is NMR-inactive.

shortQuestions: Stretching vibration: the atoms move along the bond axis so the bond length increases and decreases periodically; it may be symmetric or asymmetric.

Bending vibration: the bond angle changes while bond lengths stay the same — scissoring and rocking (in-plane), wagging and twisting (out-of-plane). Stretching needs more energy, so it absorbs at higher wavenumbers than bending.
Transmittance 100% means that all the incident radiation passes through the sample at that wavelength — nothing is absorbed.
So the compound has no bond or group that absorbs at that frequency (it is transparent there). If the whole spectrum shows 100% transmittance, the compound does not absorb in that region at all.
λmax is the wavelength at which a substance shows its maximum absorbance in its absorption (e.g. UV-visible) spectrum.

It is characteristic of the chromophore (absorbing group) and helps to identify the compound; measurements for concentration are made at λmax because sensitivity is greatest there (e.g. β-carotene, KMnO₄ at 525 nm).
Beer–Lambert law: the absorbance of a solution is directly proportional to the concentration of the absorbing substance and to the path length of light through it: A = log(I₀/I) = εbc.

Here I₀ is the incident intensity, I the transmitted intensity, ε the molar absorptivity (a constant for the substance at that wavelength), b the path length (cm) and c the molar concentration. Measuring A at λmax therefore gives the concentration (using a calibration graph).
Tetramethylsilane, Si(CH₃)₄, has twelve equivalent protons, so it gives one sharp, strong signal.
Silicon is less electronegative than carbon, so these protons are highly shielded and absorb upfield of almost all organic protons; the TMS signal is taken as δ = 0.
TMS is also chemically inert, non-polar, soluble in most organic solvents and volatile (b.p. 27 °C), so it is easily removed after the measurement.

In the ionisation chamber the vaporised sample is bombarded by a beam of high-energy electrons (about 70 eV). These knock electrons out of the molecules, forming positive molecular ions (M⁺) and fragment ions: M + e⁻ → M⁺ + 2e⁻.
Only charged particles can be accelerated by electric fields and deflected by magnetic fields, so ionisation is essential for separating the particles according to m/z.
Magnesium perchlorate (anhydrone) is a very strong, efficient drying agent that absorbs water vapour completely and quickly.

It does not absorb CO₂, so in combustion analysis the water is collected and weighed first, and CO₂ is absorbed separately afterwards (in NaOH); this allows hydrogen and carbon to be determined separately.
Modern (instrumental) methods are much faster and can be automated.

They need only very small amounts of sample (micrograms or less), are more sensitive and accurate, are often non-destructive, and give structural information (functional groups, connectivity, molecular mass) that classical gravimetric or volumetric methods cannot.

In the mass spectrum of an element each peak corresponds to one isotope: the number of peaks gives the number of isotopes, the m/z value gives each isotope's mass, and the peak height gives its relative abundance.
Example — chlorine: peaks at m/z 35 and 37 with heights in the ratio 3 : 1 (75% and 25%). So chlorine has two isotopes, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl, and its average atomic mass = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25)/100 = 35.5.
Nuclei with spin, such as ¹H, behave like tiny magnets. In a strong external magnetic field they line up either with the field (lower energy, α-spin) or against it (higher energy, β-spin).

When radio-frequency radiation whose energy equals the energy gap (ΔE = hν) is supplied, the nucleus absorbs it and 'flips' from the α to the β state. This absorption (resonance) is detected as an NMR signal.
longQuestions: (a) Mass spectroscopy is a technique in which molecules are converted into gaseous ions that are separated according to their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z), giving atomic and molecular masses and structural information.

Construction and working: (i) inlet system — the sample is vaporised; (ii) ionisation chamber — the vapour is bombarded with high-energy electrons, forming positive molecular and fragment ions; (iii) accelerating plates — an electric field accelerates the ions into a narrow beam; (iv) analyser — a magnetic field deflects the ions into circular paths, r = mv/(qB), so ions of different m/z follow different paths; varying B or V brings each kind of ion in turn onto the detector; (v) detector — the ion current is amplified and recorded as a mass spectrum (relative abundance against m/z).

(b) Element: each peak is an isotope; the m/z values give isotopic masses and the heights their abundances, so relative atomic mass = Σ(isotopic mass × % abundance)/100 (e.g. neon: ²⁰Ne 90.5%, ²¹Ne 0.3%, ²²Ne 9.2% → 20.18).

Compound: the molecular-ion peak M⁺ (the peak at the highest m/z, apart from small isotope peaks) gives the molecular mass; the fragment peaks (and the base peak, the tallest) give clues to the structure, e.g. CH₃⁺ at 15, C₂H₅⁺ at 29.

(a) Atomic emission spectroscopy: atoms are excited (in a flame, arc or plasma); as they return to lower levels they emit light of characteristic wavelengths; the intensity of the emitted lines is measured (bright lines on a dark background). Atomic absorption spectroscopy: ground-state atoms in a flame absorb light of their characteristic wavelengths from an external source; the decrease in intensity (absorbance) is measured. Emission needs excited atoms; absorption uses the far more numerous ground-state atoms and is usually more sensitive.

(b) Flame photometer: the sample solution is sprayed (nebulised) into a flame; the atoms (Na, K, Li, Ca) are excited and emit their characteristic light; a filter isolates the wavelength (Na 589 nm, K 766 nm); a photocell measures the intensity, which is proportional to concentration. Atomic absorption spectrometer: a hollow-cathode lamp made of the element emits its characteristic lines, which pass through a flame (or graphite furnace) containing the atomised sample; the atoms absorb part of this light; a monochromator selects the line and a detector measures the absorbance.

(c) Qualitative analysis: the wavelengths of the emission or absorption lines are characteristic of each element (its 'fingerprint'), so they identify which elements are present. Quantitative analysis: emission intensity or absorbance is proportional to concentration (Beer–Lambert law); a calibration graph made with standard solutions gives the concentration of the unknown. Uses: Na and K in blood serum, lead and mercury in water, trace metals in soil, food and alloys.

(a) Proton NMR (¹H NMR) spectroscopy is the study of the absorption of radio-frequency radiation by hydrogen nuclei placed in a strong magnetic field. Because protons in different chemical environments absorb at slightly different frequencies, it reveals the kinds of hydrogen atoms in a molecule.

(b) Electrons around a proton circulate in the applied field and set up a small opposing field, so the nucleus feels a slightly smaller field — it is shielded. More shielded protons absorb upfield (lower chemical shift, δ). Electronegative atoms or groups (O, N, halogens, C=O) withdraw electron density and deshield the proton, which then absorbs downfield (higher δ).
Chemical shift δ (ppm) = (ν_sample − ν_TMS)/ν_spectrometer × 10⁶, with TMS at δ = 0. Typical values: C–CH₃ ≈ 0.9; CH₃–C=O ≈ 2.1; CH₃–O ≈ 3.3; aromatic H ≈ 7–8; –CHO ≈ 9–10; –COOH ≈ 10–12.

(c) Number of signals = number of chemically different kinds of protons; the position (δ) of each signal shows its environment; the area under each signal (integration) gives the relative number of protons of that kind; splitting (n + 1 rule) shows the number of neighbouring protons. Example: ethanol CH₃CH₂OH gives three signals (CH₃ triplet, CH₂ quartet, OH singlet) with areas 3 : 2 : 1.

(a) UV-visible spectroscopy is based on the absorption of ultraviolet (200–400 nm) or visible (400–800 nm) radiation by molecules, which promotes electrons from lower-energy (bonding or non-bonding) orbitals to higher-energy (antibonding) orbitals. A spectrophotometer (deuterium/tungsten lamp, monochromator, quartz cell, detector) records absorbance against wavelength; λmax and the molar absorptivity are characteristic of the chromophore (C=C, C=O, conjugated systems, aromatic rings). Conjugation lowers the energy gap and shifts λmax to longer wavelengths. Absorbance obeys the Beer–Lambert law, so concentrations can be measured.

(b) Electronic transitions in organic molecules: σ → σ* — in saturated compounds (alkanes); needs very high energy (λ < 150 nm, far UV). n → σ* — in compounds with lone pairs on O, N, S or halogens (alcohols, amines, alkyl halides); about 150–250 nm.

π → π* — in compounds with double or triple bonds and aromatic rings (ethene ≈ 171 nm, buta-1,3-diene ≈ 217 nm); strong absorption that shifts to longer λ with conjugation. n → π* — in compounds with a lone pair on an atom that is part of a π bond (C=O of aldehydes and ketones, ≈ 280–300 nm); lowest energy and weak absorption.
Energy order: σ → σ* > n → σ* > π → π* > n → π*.

(a) Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is the study of the absorption of infrared radiation (about 4000–625 cm⁻¹) by molecules, which excites the vibrations of their bonds. Only vibrations that change the dipole moment absorb. The spectrum (% transmittance against wavenumber) shows which bonds and functional groups are present.

(b) Molecular vibrations: stretching — the bond length changes along the bond axis; symmetric (both bonds stretch together) or asymmetric (one stretches as the other contracts). Bending — the bond angle changes; in-plane scissoring and rocking, out-of-plane wagging and twisting. A non-linear molecule of N atoms has 3N − 6 fundamental vibrations (3N − 5 if linear); e.g. H₂O has 3 and CO₂ has 4.

(c) Functional-group region (4000–1500 cm⁻¹): absorptions here are characteristic of particular bonds — O–H (3200–3600, broad), N–H (3300–3500), C–H (2850–3100), C≡N (≈ 2250), C≡C (2100–2260), C=O (1650–1750, strong), C=C (1620–1680) — so it identifies the functional groups present.

Fingerprint region (1500–625 cm⁻¹): a complicated pattern of bending and skeletal (C–C, C–O, C–N) vibrations that is unique to each compound; comparing it with the spectrum of a known sample confirms the identity of the compound, just as a fingerprint identifies a person.
